title: Orientation
body: You have probably given a presentation before, whether at school, in a group, or in front of a class. At university, presentations are used differently. They are a form of assessment, with marking criteria attached, and they take several forms depending on what your tutor wants to test. This lesson looks at what those forms are and why presenting matters beyond the mark.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: identify the main types of presentation you may be asked to give, and describe where presenting is used beyond assessment.

title: Concept introduction
body: A presentation tests many of the same things a written assignment does. You still need an argument, evidence, and a clear line of reasoning. What changes is how you deliver it. You speak rather than write, an audience is in front of you, and you usually need visual aids as well. Constraints matter too: a time limit, sometimes a slide limit, and questions at the end that you cannot predict. Tutors assess your content, your communication, your delivery, your visual aids, and how you handle those questions.

title: Types of presentation
instruction: Select each type to find out more.

_items.title: Individual
_items.body: The most common form. You research, build and deliver a presentation on your own, usually to a seminar or tutorial group. If the task is formative, you get feedback you can use next time. Research-focused versions ask you to report on your methodology, findings and conclusions so far.

_items.title: Poster
_items.body: Used increasingly, because posters are how research gets shared at academic conferences. You condense a whole study onto one surface: the problem, key literature, method, findings, conclusion. The difficulty is visual as much as academic. You have to summarise without losing rigour, and you have to build it in software that may be unfamiliar.

_items.title: Group
_items.body: A common source of anxiety, and used deliberately: tutors want you to develop the interpersonal skills employers look for. The challenge is getting every member to contribute, then reconciling those contributions into something coherent. Preparation matters more here than anywhere else. Nominating a leader who delegates by preference and skillset is one way to manage it.

_items.title: Professional or practice-based
_items.body: Used in vocational subjects to mirror what you will actually do at work. A marketing student pitches to prospective clients. A social work student presents recommendations on a difficult case. A sport science student presents a coaching plan. Tutors may assess professional standards and ethical awareness alongside the presentation itself.

_items.title: Interview-based
_items.body: Closer to a conversation than a talk. A tutor engages you in dialogue to test how deep your understanding goes. It works like a job interview, and it resembles the viva voce that PhD students face after submitting a thesis.

_items.title: Technology-based
_items.body: Delivered through digital platforms, either live via Teams or Zoom, or recorded as video. Assessment focuses on whether you can hold a remote audience, and on your digital skills: integrating audio, video, animation or interactivity into something that still communicates clearly.

title: Practical guidance
body: Presenting is not only an assessment task. Employers test communication at interview, and often that means a presentation on a general topic. They care less about the content than about how you handle yourself. They are looking for evidence that you can explain complex material to people who do not share your expertise. That skill transfers into almost every profession. It is worth treating each presentation task on your course as practice for that, rather than as a hurdle to clear. Whatever the type, read the instructions and the marking criteria carefully before you start. They tell you what the tutor is actually assessing.

title: Summary
body: Presentations at university come in several forms, and each one tests something slightly different. What they share is that your communication is being assessed, not just what you know. The next lesson looks at how to work out what a particular brief is asking of you.

title: Orientation
body: Every presentation task starts with a brief. It might be a paragraph in a module handbook or a page in an assignment specification. Either way, it is doing two jobs at once: telling you what you must do, and leaving other things for you to decide. Reading it properly means separating those two.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: identify what a presentation brief requires you to do, and distinguish those requirements from the choices it leaves to you.

title: Concept introduction
body: A brief contains requirements and choices, and they are not always signposted. Requirements are the things you cannot change: the format, the time limit, the elements that must appear. Choices are everything else: which topic, which evidence, how you structure the argument. Students who read only for the requirements end up doing the minimum. Students who miss them lose marks for something they never noticed. The example below is an individual presentation, but the same reading applies whatever the type.

title: The brief
instruction: Select each marked phrase to see the commentary.

_passage.text: [UNMERGED: brief content comes from the context pack]

title: Practical guidance
body: Read the brief twice before you start. The first time, mark everything you must do. The second time, mark everything it does not say: those are your decisions to make, and they are where the marks above a pass usually sit. If the marking criteria are published separately, read those alongside the brief. They often tell you what the brief only implies.

title: Check
body: A brief says: 'Your presentation must include at least one example from published research.' Which of the following is true?
instruction: Select one option, then Submit.

_items.text: Including a research example is a requirement; which example you choose is yours to decide.
_items.feedback: Correct. The brief requires at least one example from published research, but it does not say which one. The requirement is fixed; the choice of example is yours.

_items.text: You must use the example your tutor recommends.
_items.feedback: The brief does not mention a tutor's recommendation. It requires an example from published research but leaves the choice to you.

_items.text: Including a research example is optional because the brief says 'at least one'.
_items.feedback: 'At least one' means one is the minimum, not that it is optional. The brief requires at least one example; you could include more, but you cannot include none.

_items.text: You should include as many examples as possible to show breadth.
_items.feedback: The brief says 'at least one', which sets a minimum, not a target. More examples are allowed but not required, and adding too many may crowd out other required elements.

title: Summary
body: A brief tells you what is required and leaves the rest to you. Reading for both is the difference between meeting the task and doing well at it. The next lesson looks at what to do once you know what is being asked: research and planning.

title: Orientation
body: Between reading a brief and writing your first slide there is a gap. It is where most of the work happens, and it is where most of the time gets lost. This lesson is about what goes in that gap.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: describe the steps between receiving a brief and having a workable plan, and recognise what makes a plan usable.

title: Concept introduction
body: Planning is not the same as thinking about it. A plan is something you can work from: it tells you what each section covers, what evidence goes where, and whether you have met the brief. Research comes first, but research without a question tends to sprawl. The trick is to know what you are looking for before you start looking.

title: Practical guidance
body: A usable plan has three things. It names each section. It says what goes in each one, in enough detail that you could start writing from it tomorrow. And it can be checked against the brief, point by point, to confirm nothing required is missing. If your plan is a list of topics, it is not finished. If you could hand it to someone else and they could build roughly the right presentation from it, it is.

title: Summary
body: Planning turns a brief into something you can build from. The steps are ordinary: questions, sources, selective reading, a shape, a check. Skipping them costs more time than doing them. The next lesson looks at what goes on the slides.

title: Orientation
body: Slides are the part of a presentation people remember getting wrong. Too much text, read aloud, in a font nobody at the back can see. This lesson is about what slides are for, and how to tell when they are working.

title: Learning outcomes
body: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to: distinguish a visual aid that carries a point from one that carries a script, and recognise features that make a slide or poster support the speaker.

title: Concept introduction
body: A visual aid supports what you are saying. It does not say it for you. That distinction decides most of what goes on a slide: if the slide carries your script, the audience reads it and stops listening, and you end up reading aloud to people who are ahead of you. If it carries the point, the audience looks, understands, and comes back to you for the rest. The same applies to a poster, where the reader is on their own and the design has to do more.

title: Weak and strong slides
instruction: Select the arrows to compare the two slides.
mobileInstruction: Select the plus icon followed by the arrow to compare the two slides.

_items.title: Too much on the slide
_items.body: Six bullet points, each a full sentence. The presenter reads them aloud. The audience finishes reading before the presenter finishes speaking, so they are waiting rather than listening. Nothing here needs to be a slide: it is a script that has been made visible.

_graphic.alt: A presentation slide headed 'Social media strategy', filled with six bullet points, each a full sentence in small text. The text fills the slide edge to edge.

_items.title: Enough to anchor the point
_items.body: Three short phrases with room around them. The audience reads them in a couple of seconds and looks back at the speaker, who supplies the detail. The slide holds the structure; the speaker holds the content.

_graphic.alt: A presentation slide headed 'Three channels, one voice' with three short phrases in large text. White space surrounds the content.

title: Practical guidance
body: Before a slide is finished, check three things. Can someone at the back read it? Could you deliver the point without the slide in front of you, using it only as a prompt? And is anything on it there for decoration rather than meaning? If a slide fails the second test, it is carrying your script. Move the words into your notes and leave the slide with the point.

title: Check
body: A slide contains six bullet points, each a full sentence, which the presenter reads aloud. What is the main problem?
instruction: Select one option, then Submit.

_items.text: The audience reads ahead instead of listening
_items.feedback: Correct. When the slide contains what the presenter is about to say, the audience reads it faster than the presenter can speak. They finish before the speaker does, so they are waiting rather than listening. The slide is carrying the script instead of supporting the speaker.

_items.text: The font is likely too small
_items.feedback: Small fonts are a problem, but they are a symptom here rather than the main issue. Six full sentences require small text to fit on a slide. The deeper problem is that the slide is trying to carry the whole script.

_items.text: Too many slides
_items.feedback: The question describes one slide with too much content, not too many slides. The problem is what is on this slide, not the number of slides.

_items.text: The presenter has not rehearsed
_items.feedback: Reading aloud from slides is often a sign of under-rehearsal, but the main problem here is the slide design. Even a well-rehearsed presenter cannot stop an audience reading ahead when the slide shows the whole script.

title: Summary
body: A visual aid earns its place by supporting the speaker rather than replacing them. Fewer words, larger text, and nothing on the slide that does not carry meaning. The last lesson looks at how to structure what you say.

title: Orientation
body: An essay can afford a slow start. A presentation cannot. Your audience decides in the first thirty seconds whether they are going to follow you, and once they have drifted you rarely get them back. This lesson is about the shape that stops that happening.

title: Learning outcomes
body:
By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • Describe the hook-body-conclusion structure.
  • Explain how a conclusion that returns to the objectives closes the argument.

title: The three-part structure
body: Presentations have three parts. The hook gives the audience a reason to listen, in the first minute, before you have earned their attention any other way. The body carries the argument, in an order the audience can follow without a page to turn back to. The conclusion returns to what the brief asked for and shows that you have done it. That last part is the one most often skipped. A presentation that summarises its points and stops has told the audience what it said. A presentation that returns to the objectives has told them why it mattered.

title: Structuring a presentation
body: [UNMERGED: structureBody]
instruction: [UNMERGED: structureInstruction]

title: Practical guidance
body: Check the structure before you build the slides. Read your plan and ask three questions. Does the opening give someone a reason to keep listening, or does it only say what the presentation is about? Can a listener follow the middle without going back? And does the ending connect to what the brief asked for, point by point? If the answer to the last one is no, you have a summary where you need a conclusion.

title: Check your understanding
body: A student ends their presentation by listing everything they covered. What is missing?
instruction: Select one option.

_items.text: A hook
_items.feedback: The hook comes at the start. The student has reached the end, so the hook has already happened or been missed earlier.

_items.text: A connection to what the brief asked for
_items.feedback: Correct. Listing what you covered is a summary. A conclusion returns to the objectives in the brief and shows that you have met them. The difference is between saying what you said and showing why it mattered.

_items.text: More content in the body
_items.feedback: The body carries the argument. Listing what you covered suggests the argument is complete; the gap is in how you close it, not whether you have enough content.

title: Reflection
body: Think about a presentation you have given or will give. What could you use as a hook in the first minute? And how would a conclusion that returns to the brief differ from a summary?

title: Summary
body: Hook, body, conclusion. The hook earns attention, the body carries the argument, and the conclusion returns to what was asked. You now have the whole process, from reading a brief to structuring what you say. The next step is practising it out loud.
